## Why this unit matters

- Chapter 8: parameters are fixed unknowns, uncertainty is sampling variability.
- **Bayesian view:** parameters are random variables; a **prior** is updated into
  a **posterior** by the data.
- Same SIR model, same reports — different treatment of uncertainty, with
  [Turing.jl](https://turinglang.org/).

::: {.notes}
The engine changes from optimisation to MCMC sampling, and the output changes
from a point estimate plus interval to a full posterior distribution.
:::

## Bayes' theorem for the SIR model

$$
p(\theta\mid y_{1:n})=\frac{p(y_{1:n}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)}{p(y_{1:n})},
$$

same Poisson likelihood as Chapter 8, with weakly informative priors on the
natural $[0,1]$ ranges:

$$
i_0\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,20),\qquad \beta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,10).
$$

The normalising constant is intractable; **NUTS** draws samples whose histogram
approximates the posterior.

::: {.notes}
Prior means $1/21\approx0.048$ and $1/11\approx0.091$ are broad near the truth
($i_0=0.01,\beta=0.05$) but supported only on plausible values.
:::

## The probabilistic model and sampler

```{julia}
#| label: ch09-sample
#| output: false
#| warning: false
using OrdinaryDiffEq, SciMLSensitivity, Turing, MCMCChains
using Distributions, StableRNGs

function sir_ode09!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R, C = u
    β, c, γ = p
    N = S + I + R
    infection = β * c * I / N * S
    du[1] = -infection
    du[2] = infection - γ * I
    du[3] = γ * I
    du[4] = infection
end

tmax = 40.0
prob09 = ODEProblem(sir_ode09!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0], (0.0, tmax), [0.05, 10.0, 0.25])
sol = solve(prob09, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0)
incidence = Array(sol)[4, 2:end] .- Array(sol)[4, 1:(end - 1)]
data = rand.(StableRNG(20240607), Poisson.(incidence))

@model function bayes_sir(y, prob)
    l = length(y)
    i₀ ~ Beta(1.0, 20.0)
    β ~ Beta(1.0, 10.0)
    I = i₀ * 1000.0
    prob = remake(prob; u0 = [1000.0 - I, I, 0.0, 0.0], p = [β, 10.0, 0.25],
        tspan = (0.0, float(l)))
    sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0)
    SciMLBase.successful_retcode(sol) || (Turing.@addlogprob! -Inf; return nothing)
    C = Array(sol)[4, :]
    X = C[2:end] .- C[1:(end - 1)]
    for i in 1:l
        y[i] ~ Poisson(max(X[i], 0.0) + 1e-6)
    end
end

chain = sample(StableRNG(2), bayes_sir(data, prob09), NUTS(0.8),
    MCMCSerial(), 300, 2; chain_type = MCMCChains.Chains, progress = false)
```

```{julia}
#| label: ch09-diagnostics
(max_rhat = round(maximum(rhat(chain).nt.rhat); digits = 3),
 posterior_mean = (i₀ = round(mean(vec(Array(chain[:, :i₀, :]))); digits = 4),
                   β = round(mean(vec(Array(chain[:, :β, :]))); digits = 4)),
 truth = (i₀ = 0.01, β = 0.05))
```

::: {.notes}
Three hundred draws over two chains run fast enough to demonstrate live while
still giving a meaningful $\hat R$. Say out loud that a real analysis wants more.
NUTS differentiates through the ODE solve via `SciMLSensitivity`.
:::

## Posterior and predictive check

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch09-posterior
#| fig-cap: "Left: marginal posteriors (blue) around the truth (red). Right: 95% posterior predictive band vs the data (grey)."
using CairoMakie
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
i0s = vec(Array(chain[:, :i₀, :]))
βs = vec(Array(chain[:, :β, :]))

function incidence_at(i₀, β, l)
    I = i₀ * 1000.0
    solp = solve(remake(prob09; u0 = [1000.0 - I, I, 0.0, 0.0],
        p = [β, 10.0, 0.25], tspan = (0.0, float(l))), Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0)
    C = Array(solp)[4, :]
    C[2:end] .- C[1:(end - 1)]
end
l = length(data); obstimes = 1.0:1.0:tmax
idx = rand(StableRNG(3), 1:length(βs), 150)
curves = reduce(hcat, [incidence_at(i0s[k], βs[k], l) for k in idx])
lo = [quantile(curves[t, :], 0.025) for t in 1:l]
hi = [quantile(curves[t, :], 0.975) for t in 1:l]
md = [quantile(curves[t, :], 0.5) for t in 1:l]

fig09 = Figure(size = (900, 360))
axd = Axis(fig09[1, 1]; xlabel = "value", ylabel = "density", title = "Marginals")
density!(axd, i0s; color = (:steelblue, 0.4), strokecolor = :steelblue, strokewidth = 2)
density!(axd, βs; color = (:darkorange, 0.4), strokecolor = :darkorange, strokewidth = 2)
vlines!(axd, [0.01, 0.05]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2)
axp = Axis(fig09[1, 2]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "new cases/day",
    title = "Posterior predictive")
band!(axp, collect(obstimes), lo, hi; color = (:steelblue, 0.3))
lines!(axp, collect(obstimes), md; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3)
scatter!(axp, collect(obstimes), data; color = :grey20)
fig09
```

::: {.notes}
The predictive band envelops the data; the marginals concentrate around the
truth. The book chapter also shows trace plots and full $\hat R$ / ESS tables.
:::

## Takeaways and limitations

- `@model` + `NUTS` turns Bayes' theorem into executable sampling.
- Check convergence with $\hat R\approx1$ and effective sample size.
- Priors are modelling choices; guard the ODE solve and floor the rate.
- NUTS re-solves + differentiates the ODE each step — costlier than Chapter 8.
- $\beta$–$c$ non-identifiability persists; Poisson still assumes equidispersion.

Read the [book chapter](../../chapters/09-bayesian-inference.html); see
[Turing.jl](https://turinglang.org/) and
[MCMCChains.jl](https://turinglang.org/MCMCChains.jl/stable/).

::: {.notes}
The central advantage: Bayesian inference makes assumptions explicit and
propagates them directly into the posterior predictive distribution.
:::
